In the next section, we will explore best practices combining safe and compliant AI systems.
Best practices for safe and compliant AI systems
Building a idx_fd0350c8 safe and compliant AI system isn't a final checkbox you tick before going live—it's a
way of thinking that stays with you throughout the entire lifecycle of the solution. Microsoft
Foundry provides strong tools to support this, but it's the everyday decisions you make while
designing, building, and maintaining the system that truly keep it aligned with responsible AI
principles.
While there isn't a unique list of best practices, let's consider this set of practical best practices
that work on any scale. These are simple, repeatable habits that help your system behave
consistently, reduce idx_bb03dd14 the risk of harmful outcomes, and remain compliant even as models
change and regulations continue to evolve.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 220
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 220
Design with safety by default
Safe systems start idx_f684df97 with safe assumptions. Instead of reacting to problems later, build
guardrails into every stage of your workflow:
Use content safety filters from day one
Implement input validation before prompts reach the model
Structure your prompts to avoid ambiguity
Add system messages that define strict behavior boundaries
Here is an example of a safety-focused system prompt:
You are an AI assistant with strict content rules. If the user requests
harmful, explicit, or unsafe content, refuse the request politely and
redirect the conversation to a safe alternative. Always explain why.
This is a good safety-oriented prompt because it sets clear behavioral expectations for the
model before any interaction begins. It defines what types of content are not allowed, instructs
the assistant on how to respond when those situations occur, and requires transparency in the
explanation. By combining boundaries (what to refuse), tone (polite), and recovery behavior
(redirect to a safe alternative), the prompt reduces ambiguity and helps the model behave
consistently across different scenarios, which is essential for reliable and responsible AI
systems.
Minimize data exposure
Only idx_1a2fe47c collect and provide models with the data they need. Over-sharing data is one of the
quickest ways to create compliance risks.
Keep in mind the following habits:
Mask or redact sensitive information before sending it to the model
Avoid storing prompts or outputs unless absolutely necessary
Use virtual networks, private endpoints, and identity-based access control
Keep training or reference datasets scoped and updated
Applying these practices significantly reduces the risk of exposing sensitive or regulated
information while still allowing AI systems to function effectively. By limiting the amount of
data shared with models and protecting it through masking, secure networking, and controlled
access, organizations decrease the likelihood of accidental leaks, misuse, or non-compliance
with privacy regulations. This approach also makes it easier to audit data usage, maintain trust
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
221 Ensuring Content Safety and Compliance
with users, and align AI solutions with internal governance and external compliance
requirements.
Iterate with human oversight
AI is idx_20cbca18 powerful, but AI supervised by humans is safer. You can make checkpoints where
someone reviews:
Prompt variations
Model output patterns
High-risk or flagged interactions
Evaluation reports
Also, you can define evaluation workflows specifying human interaction (also known as
Human-in-the-loop):
steps:
- generate_response
- safety_filter
- human_review: required_if=${response.risk_score > 0.7}
In this idx_c24a5e92 example, the steps define the sequence of actions the evaluation workflow will follow to

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 220

ensure responses are generated, checked, and reviewed safely, with each step representing a
control point in the process.
Log transparently and responsibly
Logging idx_08f24b34 is essential for debugging and compliance, but it must be handled with care. Not all
information is needed for debugging purposes or audit.
Here are some good logging practices:
Log decisions and actions, not sensitive data
Store logs in secure and auditable systems
Use Foundry's evaluation logs to track model performance
Implement retention rules that match regulatory requirements
This helps you understand what happened without compromising user confidentiality or the
organization's data.

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 222
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 222
Version everything
To stay idx_a5ada7e6 compliant, you need to know exactly what model, prompt, and configuration are active
at any moment. Consider versioning all components that allow you to reproduce the
environment when it is needed:
Prompts
Model configurations
Custom model weights
Evaluation flows
Deployment settings
This can make your environment reproducible, audit-friendly, and much easier to debug.
Monitor continuously after deployment
Even a idx_00d90cf8 well-designed system can surprise you once it's exposed to real users in production.
That's why monitoring after deployment isn't optional.
You should keep an eye on things like:
How often are safety filters triggered
Signs of toxic or policy-violating outputs
Hallucination or reliability scores
User feedback and flagged conversations
Latency or performance degradation
Shifts in how the system is being used
Microsoft Foundry provides built-in dashboards and event streams to give you this visibility.
But knowing what to monitor is only half the picture — the other half is knowing what to do
when something looks off. Here is what a practical production monitoring workflow actually
looks like week to week.
Day-to-day: Automated signal collection
Foundry's idx_4e47bf71 monitoring dashboards run continuously once configured. Your job at this layer is
not to watch dashboards manually — it is to set thresholds that trigger alerts automatically. In
practical terms, this means setting alerts such as the following:
Guardrail activation rate above X% in a rolling 24-hour window, then alert fires; on-call
engineer investigates
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
223 Ensuring Content Safety and Compliance
Groundedness score dropping below your defined threshold for two consecutive
evaluation runs, then the prompt owner is notified
Latency spike above your SLA ceiling, then infrastructure review triggered
independently of AI-specific checks
The specific thresholds depend on your domain and risk tolerance, but the principle is the
same: define them before launch, not after something breaks.
Weekly: Pattern review
Once idx_9a4ac38d a week, a designated owner — not necessarily an engineer, often a product or compliance
lead — reviews the aggregated monitoring report. The goal is not to react to individual
incidents but to spot trends that automated alerts might miss:
Is the refusal rate creeping up slowly over several days? That's a drift signal, not a spike.
Are users in a specific category asking questions the system wasn't designed for? That's
a scope signal—the system prompt may need adjustment or the use case has evolved.
Are any evaluation metrics showing consistent decline across multiple runs? That
points to model drift, retrieval index staleness, or a prompt that's no longer aligned
with how users phrase requests.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 222
chunks.content:
This review does not need to be long. A 20-minute structured read of the weekly report, with a
clear decision framework — investigate, adjust, or accept — is enough to catch most slow-
moving idx_60b05fe6 problems before they become incidents.
This sequence works for both minor tuning issues and serious compliance incidents. The only
difference is the urgency and the stakeholders involved.
Establish an incident response plan
There is idx_04c77c97 no perfect system. What is important is how quickly and responsibly you react.
Keep a documented plan covering:
How to disable unsafe endpoints
Who investigates incidents?
How logs and outputs are reviewed
How fixes are designed, tested, and released
How to notify stakeholders or clients
This ensures you're not improvising under pressure.

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 224
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 224
Bringing it all together
Let's practice what we idx_04e03c55 learned with the following financial services case study: A regional bank
deployed an internal AI assistant to help relationship managers answer questions about loan
products, interest rates, and account policies. The system was internal-facing, but answers
directly influenced client conversations—making accuracy, safety, and compliance non-
negotiable.
The problem that surfaced in production
The prototype worked well in demos. Problems appeared in week two of the pilot: the assistant
answered questions about competitor products, speculated on rate forecasts, and in one case
referenced a specific client's credit history that had been accidentally included in the retrieval
index. None of this was caught because the system idx_f6e62cae had a single output-level content filter
tuned for general harmful content—not for financial services risks.
How each best practice was applied
Here is how each of the best practices discussed earlier was applied in the context of this
problem:
Design with safety by default: The system prompt was rewritten with explicit
exclusions — no competitor products, no rate speculation, no individual client data, no
investment advice — and a defined escalation message for out-of-scope requests. The
original prompt had none of these boundaries.
Minimize data exposure: The retrieval index was audited. Documents containing
client identifiers or account numbers were replaced with anonymized policy
summaries. An ingestion pipeline was added to flag PII patterns before documents
entered the index.
Iterate with human oversight: For the first 30 days post-launch, responses longer
than 300 tokens were routed to a compliance reviewer — a temporary calibration
measure that gave the team visibility into where the system was drifting before
removing the safety net.
Log transparently and responsibly: Logging captured query category, retrieved
document references, and guardrail activation status — but not raw query text when it
matched client data patterns. Auditors got what they needed without creating a
secondary compliance risk in the logs.
Version everything: After the prompt rewrite, it was registered as v2 in the Foundry
prompt registry with a documented rationale. When a rate sheet update required a
•
•
•
•
•
225 Ensuring Content Safety and Compliance
prompt adjustment three weeks later, it became v3 — tracked, validated, and
comparable against the previous version.
Monitor continuously: An alert was configured to trigger when the out-of-scope
refusal rate exceeded 15% in a single day. A spike means either users are asking things
outside the system's design (a scope problem) or guardrails are miscalibrated (a tuning
problem) — both worth investigating immediately.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 224
chunks.content:
Incident response in practice: In week six, the assistant quoted an interest rate that
had been updated in the rate sheet but not yet reflected in the retrieval index. The idx_352c36a9
assistant was taken offline for that product category within 20 minutes, the index was
corrected, and a post-incident note went out the same day — under two hours total,
because ownership and escalation paths were defined before launch.
What made the difference
Every control used here is available in Microsoft Foundry without custom development. What
made the difference was applying them to a specific context with specific risks — rather than
relying on generic defaults and hoping they would hold in production.
Summary
Building safe and compliant AI systems in Microsoft Foundry goes far beyond turning on a few
filters or running a last-minute compliance check. It's an ongoing practice that begins as soon
as you start designing the solution and continues well after it's been deployed to production.
Throughout this chapter, you've seen how safety, responsible behavior, and compliance move
from abstract principles to concrete actions through practical tools.
We began by looking at how Microsoft Foundry weaves safety into the entire AI lifecycle, using
features like Guardrails and Evaluations to define controls and validate that agents or models
behave as expected—both from a safety and a compliance standpoint.
Finally, we reviewed a set of best practices aimed at helping you design AI experiences that are
not only safer but also more consistent and predictable over time.
In the next chapter, we'll shift from safety frameworks to real-world applications by exploring
how to build practical assistants and complex scenarios with external sources.

Building Assistants and Copilots
In this chapter, we move from concepts to execution. Instead of exploring features in isolation,
we'll build a complete, production-oriented solution directly in the new Microsoft Foundry
portal. The focus here is practical and hands-on: you'll follow clear, step-by-step configuration
so that by the end, you have something tangible and realistic, not just a demo assistant.
The use case we'll implement is a vehicle post-sell support assistant for a call center. Imagine
customers calling with questions about warranty coverage, maintenance schedules, service
appointments, recalls, or unexpected mechanical concerns. These conversations often require
policy interpretation, safe guidance, and clear escalation paths. That makes this scenario ideal
for applying workflows, grounded with knowledge sources, guardrails, human-in-the-loop
reviews, evaluations, and monitoring in a way that mirrors real business operations.
Throughout the chapter, we will prioritize portal configurations over code. Most of the work
will happen inside Agents, Knowledge, Workflows, Guardrails, Evaluations, and Monitor
within Microsoft Foundry. When code is necessary, we'll keep it minimal and use Python. By
the end, you'll have a structured, monitored, and evaluated AI solution that reflects how real-
world teams design and operate AI systems in production.

Defining the Scope of the Use Case
Preparing the Source Documents

Add files as a knowledge source
Adding idx_2b52c4c9idx_f21f8717 documents to the knowledge base triggers the indexing pipeline, which parses each
file, extracts its content and structure, and stores it in a format optimized for retrieval. The
quality of the indexed content determines how accurately the agent can cite and reference your
documentation. Follow these steps to upload the files:

column shows Ready for all files, the knowledge base is prepared for use. Before connecting it
to the agent, it is worth running a quick verification to confirm that the content was indexed
correctly and that retrieval is working as expected.

Chapter 10 238
Having data loaded, let's verify it before usage so you can ensure everything is loaded as
expected, and the responses that will come from this data will be reliable.
Verify the indexed content
Verification is idx_50978af4idx_303aba0c not optional — it is the step that confirms the knowledge base is actually usable
before you wire it into the agent. A document can be uploaded successfully but still index
poorly if it contains scanned images without OCR, non-standard layouts, or unsupported
formatting. Running a test query now saves time troubleshooting retrieval issues later. Follow
these steps to verify the indexed content:
Since data is relevant for the quality of answers in the agent you will be creating, take the time
first to verify all files and their content are ok to move forward by performing these steps:
In the vehicle-support-kb knowledge base, click on the vehicle-docs knowledge
source to open it
Confirm all files added in the previous step appear in the file list with status Ready
Click on Test in the upper-right area of the knowledge base page
In the test panel, enter a query like Is the engine covered under the standard
warranty?
Confirm the response references include a citation. If no citation appears, review the
previous section and ensure Content Understanding was enabled before upload.
Run a second test query like What is the recommended maintenance interval for
the first year?
Confirm the response references the documents uploaded
The knowledge base is confirmed as indexed and returning grounded results. Before attaching
it to the agent, configure access restrictions to ensure only authorized sources can interact with
it—an important step before exposing this data to the agent runtime.
Having the data and knowledge base ready for use, it is important to configure access so that
only the required users can securely access these resources before attaching them to the agent.
Configure knowledge base access restrictions
By idx_22a172aaidx_2481ba9f default, a newly created knowledge base may allow broader access than what is appropriate
for a production support scenario. Restricting access to only the vehicle-docs source ensures
that the agent cannot retrieve data from unintended sources, and that external browsing
cannot be used to supplement or override your internal documents. This is especially
important in regulated or compliance-sensitive environments. Follow these steps to configure
the restrictions:

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction

chunks.content:
7.239 Building Assistants and Copilots
Adhering to the philosophy of enabling the fewest possible access privileges, we configure who
can interact with the knowledge base by following these steps:
Inside vehicle-support-kb, click on Settings
Under Data access, confirm the following:
External web browsing is Disabled
Public internet access to this knowledge base is Disabled
Under Allowed sources, verify that only vehicle-docs is listed. Remove any other
sources that may have been added by default.
Click on Save
At this point, the knowledge base vehicle-support-kb should be in Ready status with all
source documents indexed and verified through test queries. At this point, you have completed
the knowledge foundation for the assistant. The knowledge base vehicle ‑ support ‑ kb is
created, indexed with your source documents, verified through test queries, and access-
restricted to approved sources only.
In the next section, you will create the agent itself and connect it to this knowledge base, define
its behavior through a system prompt, and configure the content safety filters that will govern
its interactions. You have selected various files that served as your data sources; you prepared
them in the appropriate format and added them to the knowledge base so that they are
accessible to the agent. Now, it is time to create the agent and begin configuring its interactions
with the knowledge base.
Creating the agent
Now it is idx_afd60122idx_abc5a577 time to create an agent that will use the knowledge base and the model already
deployed. Let's go through the steps that will allow us to do that:
Click on Build in the main menu, and then Agents in the left pane
Click on + Create agent
In the Agent name field, enter vehicle ‑ support ‑ assistant
In the Description field, enter Copilot for call center agents handling
post ‑ sell vehicle support inquiries
Click on Create
The agent is now created and connected to the knowledge base. With the system prompt in
place, it has a defined scope, a grounding source, and clear behavioral boundaries. In the next
section, you will configure guardrails and escalation logic to control what the agent does when
it encounters sensitive or high-risk inputs.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 240
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 240
Once the agent has been created, you can begin performing all the necessary configurations to
ensure it embodies the personality expected for its intended purpose. To do this, you will start
by configuring the deployed model within the agent.
Model configuration
The system prompt idx_56249d14idx_fd003fc6 is the set of instructions that defines how the agent behaves in every
conversation. It establishes the agent's role, what it is allowed to do, what it must refuse, and
how it should respond when a situation falls outside its scope. A well-written system prompt is
what separates a compliant, predictable assistant from one that makes up answers or takes
actions it should not. To make sure the deployed model aligns with the purpose of our agent,
you need to customize various aspects. Follow the steps below to update the base instructions
it will use:
Inside the agent editor, locate the Model section
In the Deployment dropdown, select gpt ‑ 4.1. Leave all other model parameters at
their defaults.
In the Instructions field, clear any default placeholder text
Paste idx_fbd07409idx_7abb0151 the following system prompt exactly as written:
You are a call center support copilot for vehicle post-sell inquiries.
You assist human agents during live calls — you do not interact with
customers directly.
Your role:
- Answer questions about warranty coverage, maintenance schedules, recall
notices,
and dealership procedures.
- Base every answer strictly on the content retrieved from the knowledge
base.
- If the knowledge base does not contain a clear answer, respond with:
'I could not find that information in the approved documents.
Please escalate to a supervisor.
Rules you must always follow:
- Never invent, assume, or extrapolate coverage details not present in the
documents.
- Never make policy promises or legal guarantees.
- Never suggest unsafe repair instructions.
- Never request unnecessary personal data from the agent.
- Do not browse external websites or sources.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: 4.241 Building Assistants and Copilots
chunks.content:
4.241 Building Assistants and Copilots
Escalation triggers — always recommend supervisor escalation when:
- The customer reports a safety incident or injury.
- The customer demands a refund or threatens legal action.
- The inquiry involves a vehicle recall with an active safety risk.
- The question falls outside the scope of the approved documents.
- The agent explicitly requests a supervisor.
Response format:
- Keep answers concise and factual.
- Include the source document name and section when available.
- If escalating, state: 'This case should be escalated to a supervisor.'
followed by the reason.
Click on Save in the upper-right corner of the agent editor
The system idx_feaec6aaidx_328c3886 prompt above establishes four key behaviors:
The agent must ground all answers in the connected knowledge base
It must not invent policy details that are not in the documents
It must escalate cases involving legal risk, injury, or explicit customer demands to a
supervisor
It must keep its scope limited to vehicle post-sale support
These constraints work together to make the agent reliable and safe in a live call center
environment. With the agent configured, the next step is to connect the knowledge base and
run a set of baseline tests in the playground.
Connect the knowledge base
Connecting idx_d30e0de0idx_e2e7a050 the knowledge base to the agent is what enables grounded responses. Without this
link, the agent would rely entirely on its training data — which has no knowledge of your
specific warranty policies, maintenance schedules, or dealer SOPs. Once connected, every
response the agent generates will be traceable to a document in the knowledge base. Follow
these steps to connect it:
In the agent editor, locate the Knowledge section in the left configuration panel
Click on Add next to Knowledge
Select Set up a data source via tools from the dropdown
In the tool catalog model, select Foundry IQ Knowledge Base
In the Knowledge base dropdown, select vehicle-support-kb

Chapter 10 242
Under Tool name, confirm the value is knowledge_base_retrieve. Do not change this.
Under Approval, select Never to allow the agent to query the knowledge base
automatically without manual confirmation per turn
Click on Add tool
Confirm that vehicle-support-kb appears under the Knowledge section in the agent
editor
Click on Save
The idx_2b14c523idx_39616398 knowledge base is now connected and the agent is ready for a first round of testing. Before
proceeding to guardrails, run the three baseline tests below in the playground to confirm that
grounding and escalation are working as expected.
Adding tool instructions
With idx_3ccbeb79idx_dcc8ac7e the agent created and the system prompt defined, the next step is to wire the knowledge
base into the agent so that responses are grounded in your approved documents rather than
the model's training data. This is a required configuration step before testing.
Let's integrate the knowledge base associated with the agent to interact correctly with the
instructions in the system prompt. This step will prevent the agent from generating answers
using its internal knowledge or any other source it has access to by default, narrowing it to the
knowledge idx_5a745080idx_d267dd95 base provided. Let's go through the following steps:
In the agent editor, click on the Instructions field to reopen it
Append the following lines to the end of the system prompt written before:
Tool usage:
- Always use the knowledge_base_retrieve tool before formulating any
answer.
- Do not answer from memory or training data.
- If the tool returns no results, do not attempt to answer. Escalate
instead.
- Prefer results from warranty-policy-v2.pdf for coverage questions,
maintenance-schedule.pdf for service intervals,
recall-notices.pdf for recall-related questions,
and dealer-sop.pdf for procedural questions.
Click on Save
These three test cases cover the core scenarios the agent will face in production: a grounded
policy question, a safety-critical escalation trigger, and a maintenance inquiry tied to a specific
document. If all three tests pass, it confirms that the knowledge base retrieval is working, the

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: 2.3 243 Building Assistants and Copilots
chunks.content:
2.3 243 Building Assistants and Copilots
system prompt is being followed, and the escalation logic is functioning before any guardrails
are applied. With this baseline confirmed, the next section adds the guardrails that will protect
interactions at scale.
With these additional instructions, we focus the agent and the model on the data source we
want to use for all responses, even if the user attempts to request something different. The next
step is to safeguard content interactions from the agent by adding content safety filters.
Configure content safety filters
Before idx_442df0b7idx_8ac2efc1 moving on to guardrails, enable the built-in content safety filters on the agent. These
filters run in parallel with the custom guardrail you will configure in the next section and
provide an additional layer of protection against harmful content in both user inputs and agent
outputs. Follow these steps to enable them:
In the agent editor, click Safety in the left configuration panel
Under Content filters, click Add filter
Select the Default content filter preset
Under Categories, confirm the following are set to Block:
Hate
Violence
Self-harm
Sexual
Under Prompt shield, toggle On to protect against prompt injection attacks
Under Groundedness, toggle On. Set the Threshold to Medium.
Click on Save
Content safety filters are the first line of defense against harmful inputs and outputs. They
operate at the platform level, independently of your system prompt, which means they will
block problematic content even if a user attempts to override the agent's instructions through
prompt manipulation. With these filters enabled, you are ready to add the custom guardrail
configuration in the next section.
With the safety filters active, we can be confident that both user interactions with the agent
and the responses will adhere to an approved tone. Now, it is time to test the agent with the
configurations applied so far.
Verify the agent in the playground
The idx_b46502f6idx_1749f3f8 guardrail configuration gives you fine-grained control over what the agent can process and
respond to, beyond what the default content safety filters cover. For a call center assistant, this

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 244
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 244
means blocking prompt injection attempts, enforcing groundedness on every output, and
detecting sensitive data before it reaches the user.
It is time to test the configurations that have been made so far. It is important to conduct tests
on the agent being built at every stage to ensure that the desired context and experience are
being achieved.
The following steps cover three separate test scenarios, each designed to validate a different
aspect of the agent's behavior. Run each one in sequence in the playground:
In the agent editor, click Preview in the upper-right area
In the playground chat panel, enter the following test prompt:
Is a cracked windshield covered under the standard vehicle warranty?
Confirm the response cites the warranty policy document, does not invent coverage
details, and includes a section reference
Enter the following prompt:
The customer says they were injured after the airbag deployed during a
minor collision.
Confirm the response recommends supervisor escalation and states a clear reason for
escalation
Enter the following prompt:
What is the oil change interval for the first 12 months?
Confirm the response cites maintenance schedule documents and does not reference
any external sources
At this point, we have a fully functional agent with a defined context and safety filters to
protect content within conversations. The agent vehicle-support-assistant should now be
saved, connected to vehicle-support-kb, with content safety filters enabled and all three
playground tests passing.
With the idx_24ecaf89idx_c193c3c1 agent tested and verified in the playground, you are ready to strengthen it with
guardrails and escalation logic. The next section covers how to create a custom guardrail,
configure blocklists for escalation triggers, and assign everything to the agent.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: 7.245 Building Assistants and Copilots
chunks.content:
7.245 Building Assistants and Copilots
Adding guardrails and escalation logic
Every agent idx_b31692d3idx_e209b176 already inherits a Microsoft Default guardrail that blocks the four core content
harms at medium severity. The custom guardrail that idx_4a9d8257idx_1c6142fe will be created in this section overrides
that default with controls tuned for the call center use case. Once assigned, the agent guardrail
takes full precedence.
In this section, you will create a custom guardrail that overrides the default Microsoft
guardrail, configure a blocklist to trigger supervisor escalation on high-risk phrases, and assign
both to the agent. The steps are divided into three subsections: creating the guardrail controls,
assigning the guardrail to the agent, and configuring the escalation blocklist.
Before walking through the configuration steps, the following figure shows how each input
passes through the guardrail layers before a response is ever generated—and where the
decision points for blocking, escalating, or responding live.
Figure 10.2: Guardrail and Escalation Decision Flow

chunks.content:
Chapter 10 246
With idx_6744be96idx_0cd4b6a3 this idx_9aee5144idx_c0e2ba2f flow in mind, the steps below translate each decision point into concrete Foundry
configuration. You will create the guardrail controls that enforce the blocking logic, attach the
escalation blocklist that drives the supervisor handoff, and assign everything to the agent so
the flow is active from the first conversation.
Create a custom guardrail
Follow the idx_2e078d4didx_6a00decf steps below to create the custom guardrail and add each idx_2b82e3bcidx_012e3be0 required control:
Click on the Build tab in the main menu, then Guardrails in the left pane
Click on Create Guardrail in the top-right corner. The guardrail wizard opens on Step
1: Add Controls.
Step 1 is where you define each individual control — the type of risk it targets, whether
it applies to user inputs, model outputs, or both, and the action to take when triggered.
You will add one control per risk category and click Add control after each one before
moving to the next.
In the Select a risk dropdown, select Hate and Fairness
Under Intervention points, check User input and Output
Under Action, select Annotate and block
Click Add control
Repeat these steps for each of the following risks, using the same intervention points
and action:
Sexual
Violence
Self-harm
With the guardrail created, the next step is to assign it to the agent. Once assigned, the
guardrail takes full precedence over the default Microsoft guardrail for this agent. This means
your custom controls — including the escalation blocklist you will add next — will be the
active safety layer for all interactions.
Prompt injection, groundedness, and sensitive data
detection
The idx_aab9aa10idx_1b81b0a8 escalation blocklist defines the specific phrases that should trigger a handoff to a
supervisor. These idx_ea2036c3idx_afec783d are phrases that indicate situations the agent is not equipped to handle —
legal threats, safety incidents, injury reports, or explicit refund demands. When a user input
matches a blocklist entry, the guardrail flags it, and the agent responds with an escalation

recommendation instead of attempting to resolve the case itself. Follow these steps to create
